object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged event representing something that broke and is tracked through resolution

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal from the monitoring platform (automatic) or manually raised by an engineer, that can indicate an incident

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.
raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: Customer Ticket
object_types.definition: A support ticket raised by or on behalf of a customer reporting a problem

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: The technical impact / blast radius classification of an incident

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The customer urgency / business impact classification of an incident

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: Incident State
object_types.definition: The lifecycle state of an incident

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as incident commander

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group that owns a service on a standing basis

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service that can be affected by incidents and is owned by a team

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

ambiguities.description: Nadia initially claims an incident can be noticed 'by eye' with no alert or ticket behind it, but then corrects herself to say a manual observation still creates an alert record. This self-correction suggests the boundary of what counts as an 'alert' (automatic vs. manual) may not be fully settled in practice, even though the stated rule is now firm.

source_references.excerpt: Someone noticing something by eye? It happens. ... No, actually, let me correct that. If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between 'severity change over time' and the incident record is unclear for modeling: the current severity/priority is stored on the incident, but changes are tracked only as timeline 'events' whose structure is not described. It's ambiguous whether this should be modeled as a full history/objectified fact type or left out entirely.

source_references.excerpt: Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Owen mentions a 'monitoring' state between mitigated and resolved that is used informally in practice but is explicitly excluded from the model because it's 'not in the dropdown'. This highlights a discrepancy between informal team practice and the formal system, and raises the question of whether future system changes might add this state.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is explicitly flagged as ambiguous/overloaded in team usage -- it can refer to either the Incident Commander (temporary role per incident) or the Service Owner (standing team assignment). The transcript treats these as two distinct concepts but acknowledges real-world confusion between them.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia, you said commander is a role, not a job title. Is there a different sense of owner? ... in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: 'Severity' vs 'priority' are frequently conflated by staff using the word 'sev' to mean either concept, causing real operational confusion, even though the model treats them as fully independent, mandatory, single-valued attributes.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either. Somebody says "we've got a sev one" in a channel and I don't know whether to page the whole platform team or ring one account manager.

ambiguities.description: The duplicate-of relationship's intended constraint (no chains, primary cannot itself be a duplicate) is explicitly stated as NOT enforced by the system today, meaning real data may violate the acyclic/irreflexive-chain rule. It's unclear whether the model should represent the 'intended' rule as a hard constraint or note it purely as an aspirational business rule.

source_references.excerpt: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: The final and central unresolved issue of the session: whether incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is is explicitly undecided and deferred to Ravi. No 'cause classification' concept exists in the current model, but its future addition is anticipated and disputed (Nadia wants classification/exclusion from metrics; Owen resists framing it as 'not a real incident').

source_references.excerpt: A meaningful number of those turn out to be user error ... It wasn't an incident, it was a support conversation with an incident record attached to it. ... And my position is that it absolutely was an incident. ... Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether 'Customer Ticket' (support ticket) is always literally the origin object linked to an incident, or whether 'customer report' is a broader/looser concept than the formal ticket entity with a ticket number -- Owen and Nadia use 'customer tells us' and 'customer report' informally before the formal ticket linkage requirement is clarified.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us. ... Or a customer tells us and monitoring never fires, which is the embarrassing one.
